buckets.title: Working on design
buckets.description: Improve visual polish, color usage, and component styling.

terms.title: Visual hierarchy
terms.shortDescription: Clarify the order in which elements compete for attention.
terms.definition: Visual hierarchy is the intentional use of scale, weight, color, and spacing to signal what the user should notice first, second, and last.
terms.whenToUse: Request this when a layout feels flat, when CTAs are lost, or when primary metrics are competing with secondary details.
aiPhrases: Reinforce the primary CTA so it reads as the first stop in the layout.
Dial down visual noise on secondary actions to restore hierarchy.
Use spacing and contrast to ladder information from primary to tertiary.
examples: Ask the AI to resize or recolor the hero KPI so it outranks sidebar stats.
Prompt for more whitespace above section headers to separate content blocks.

terms.title: Color intent
terms.shortDescription: Align palette choices with emotion and accessibility goals.
terms.definition: Color intent focuses on why each hue exists—reinforcing meaning, emotion, and brand credibility without sacrificing contrast.
terms.whenToUse: Use this when colors feel arbitrary, brand tones are off, or WCAG contrast is questionable.
aiPhrases: Propose a palette that signals trust first, experimentation second.
Audit accent colors for AA contrast on light and dark backgrounds.
Tie interaction states (hover, focus, active) back to the core palette.
examples: Have the AI suggest a calm neutral background for analyst dashboards.
Ask for an alert color family that is brand aligned but still high contrast.

terms.title: Component density
terms.shortDescription: Balance breathing room with information per view.
terms.definition: Component density defines how much content fits inside a module before cognitive load spikes.
terms.whenToUse: Invoke this when cards feel cramped, forms stretch too tall, or data tables lack scan anchors.
aiPhrases: Calibrate padding so cards fit three per row on desktop without crowding.
Group related form inputs to shorten the perceived path.
Introduce lightweight dividers to keep dense data scannable.

buckets.title: Working on UX
buckets.description: Clarify flows, feedback, and user confidence throughout interactions.

terms.title: Progressive disclosure
terms.shortDescription: Reveal complexity only when the user signals readiness.
terms.definition: Progressive disclosure staggers advanced controls so novice users stay focused while experts still have access on demand.
terms.whenToUse: Use when onboarding feels overwhelming or advanced toggles distract from the happy path.
aiPhrases: Gate advanced filters behind a “More options” drawer with clear affordances.
Stage the import wizard into primary vs. advanced steps with inline cues.
Surface only the top three metrics, tucking the rest under a disclosure.
examples: Request a collapsed section for power-user columns in the report builder.

terms.title: Empty state coaching
terms.shortDescription: Turn blank screens into helpful guidance.
terms.definition: Empty state coaching supplies context, example data, and a next step when there is nothing to display yet.
terms.whenToUse: Invoke when new projects start blank or data depends on upstream integrations.
aiPhrases: Draft an empty state with a single action and one sentence promise.
Show sample rows so users know what data will appear once connected.
Pair the primary CTA with a backup help link for stalled teams.

terms.title: Friction log
terms.shortDescription: Document sticking points inside the flow.
terms.definition: A friction log is a timestamped list of minor annoyances that together erode user confidence.
terms.whenToUse: Use during usability reviews when you can feel “little papercuts” slowing progress.
aiPhrases: Summarize all friction points from this flow ordered by severity.
Suggest lightweight experiments that remove two clicks from the review loop.
Translate the friction log into a prioritized bug backlog.
examples: Ask for UX copy that explains why a step is disabled instead of leaving it silent.

buckets.title: Working on structure
buckets.description: Organize layouts, grids, and content groupings for clarity.

terms.title: Information architecture
terms.shortDescription: Map relationships between pages, sections, and tasks.
terms.definition: Information architecture (IA) decides how content is chunked, labeled, and navigated so users form a reliable mental model.
terms.whenToUse: Use this when navigation feels ad hoc, users guess where to click, or content piles up without hierarchy.
aiPhrases: Propose a sitemap that keeps strategic work separate from daily tasks.
Rename navigation to reflect user intent over internal jargon.
Bundle insights, actions, and history into predictable clusters.

terms.title: Layout grid
terms.definition: A layout grid defines columns, gutters, and margins so every component aligns to a shared rhythm.
terms.whenToUse: Invoke when cards drift, typography alignment breaks, or responsive states feel improvised.
aiPhrases: Lock the desktop grid to 12 columns with 24px gutters and show how hero, cards, and footers snap to it.
Demonstrate how the grid collapses at tablet and mobile breakpoints.
Audit current screens for off-grid elements and propose fixes.
examples: Request a diagram labeling safe areas vs. bleed areas for charts.

terms.title: Content grouping
terms.shortDescription: Collect related signals so scanning becomes effortless.
terms.definition: Content grouping bundles related data points so the eye can scan one cluster at a time instead of bouncing randomly.
terms.whenToUse: Use when dashboards feel noisy, lists alternate unrelated items, or when teams mix metrics and narrative.
aiPhrases: Group health metrics separately from growth experiments in the overview.
Add clear dividers and labels when context switches.
Provide summary chips per cluster to aid quick scanning.

buckets.title: Working on content clarity
buckets.description: Sharpen copy, tone, and narrative sequencing.

terms.title: Microcopy tune-up
terms.shortDescription: Optimize short bits of UI text for tone and clarity.
terms.definition: Microcopy tune-ups adjust helper text, labels, and button copy so they reinforce intent and reduce hesitation.
terms.whenToUse: Use when tooltips ramble, CTA verbs mismatch outcomes, or helper text reads robotic.
aiPhrases: Rewrite this helper text to set expectations in under 12 words.
Offer three CTA options that emphasize momentum over obligation.
Align microcopy tone with confident, plain-spoken product language.

terms.title: Readability pass
terms.shortDescription: Ensure paragraphs are scannable and jargon free.
terms.definition: A readability pass trims dense paragraphs, swaps jargon, and improves rhythm so teams grasp the message on first read.
terms.whenToUse: Invoke when summaries get TL;DR reactions or stakeholders misinterpret plan docs.
aiPhrases: Rewrite this section at an 8th grade reading level without losing nuance.
Convert long paragraphs into a lead sentence plus bullets.
Highlight any jargon and offer plainer replacements.

terms.title: Voice consistency
terms.shortDescription: Keep tone, tense, and perspective aligned across surfaces.
terms.definition: Voice consistency ensures every touchpoint sounds like the same teammate, regardless of feature or channel.
terms.whenToUse: Use when marketing, product, and support copy feel written by different people.
aiPhrases: Audit this flow for shifts between first and second person voice.
Normalize tense and tone to match the brand voice guide.
Provide a side-by-side showing current vs. aligned voice.
examples: Ask for a quick checklist writers can run before shipping release notes.

buckets.title: Working on AI prompts
buckets.description: Shape better instructions for AI collaborators.

terms.title: Role priming
terms.shortDescription: Set context for the AI before making the ask.
terms.definition: Role priming frames who the AI should act as so responses mirror the right expertise and priorities.
terms.whenToUse: Use when answers feel generic or the AI keeps missing business context.
aiPhrases: Act as a senior product designer coaching a cross-functional trio.
Take the perspective of a UX researcher translating findings to PMs.
Respond with the bias of protecting user trust over acquisition.

terms.title: Multi-shot prompting
terms.shortDescription: Show examples of success before asking for more.
terms.definition: Multi-shot prompting feeds a few curated examples so the AI mirrors structure, tone, or level of detail in future answers.
terms.whenToUse: Invoke when outputs wobble in quality or when you need consistency across variations.
aiPhrases: Here are two sample critiques—match their depth when reviewing the next screen.
Given these example prompts, craft three more covering related scenarios.
Keep the same outline structure shown above when expanding to new use cases.

terms.title: Guardrail prompt
terms.shortDescription: Define boundaries the AI should not cross.
terms.definition: Guardrail prompts spell out failure modes, banned ideas, or privacy constraints so the AI self checks before responding.
terms.whenToUse: Use when collaborating on sensitive data, regulated content, or when the AI tends to over-promise.
aiPhrases: Never invent research data; flag any missing stats instead.
Do not recommend solutions requiring net-new ML models.
Keep all suggestions within one sprint of effort.
examples: Pair the guardrail with acceptance criteria so the AI knows when to stop ideating.
